title: WHY PETER WAS WARMING HIMSELF AT THE ENEMY’S FIRE
paragraphs:
WHY PETER WAS WARMING HIMSELF AT THE ENEMY’S FIRE
He only wanted to get warm. But before the fire went out, Peter would swear that he never knew Jesus. And the most terrifying part of the story is how easily we can find ourselves standing beside him.
There was a fire burning in the courtyard.
Nothing unusual about that.
It was cold.
Men were standing around the glowing coals, stretching their hands toward the heat while, somewhere beyond them, Jesus Christ was being questioned.
And standing among those men was Peter.
Peter.
The disciple who had walked on water.
The man who had seen the dead raised.
The man who had watched Jesus touch lepers, command storms, multiply bread, cast out demons, open blind eyes and speak words that seemed to reach into the deepest chambers of the human soul.
Peter had once looked Jesus in the face and confessed:
“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
He had promised that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
He had even drawn a sword in Gethsemane.
But now...
Peter was warming himself at somebody else’s fire.
And before you judge him, look carefully at your own hands.
Because some of us are still trying to follow Jesus while warming ourselves beside fires built by a world that does not know Him.
John records the scene with almost painful simplicity:
“Now the servants and officers who had made a fire of coals stood there, for it was cold, and they warmed themselves. And Peter stood with them and warmed himself.”
John 18:18.
The Greek makes one detail especially vivid.
The expression translated “fire of coals” or “charcoal fire” contains the word ἀνθρακιά — anthrakia.
A charcoal fire.
Peter was cold.
That matters because Scripture does not portray Peter as a cartoon villain who suddenly decided he hated Jesus.
Peter was frightened.
Confused.
Physically cold.
Emotionally overwhelmed.
He had just watched the One he believed was the Messiah allow Himself to be arrested.
Everything Peter thought was about to happen seemed to be collapsing.
Only hours earlier, he had been ready to fight.
Now he was trying to disappear into a crowd.
That is often how spiritual compromise begins.
Not with someone waking up one morning and announcing, “Today I am going to betray Jesus.”
It begins with exhaustion.
Fear.
Loneliness.
Disappointment.
A need to belong.
A desire to survive.
A little warmth.
A little acceptance.
A little relief.
Peter did not necessarily approach that fire because he wanted to become one of Christ’s enemies.
He approached because he was cold.
And that is what makes this passage so frighteningly human.
Sometimes the wrong fire feels good.
Sometimes compromise is warm.
Sometimes the place slowly pulling your heart away from Christ does not initially feel dangerous.
It feels comforting.
It feels like friendship.
It feels like attention.
It feels like being understood.
It feels like finally being accepted.
It feels like scrolling because you are lonely.
It feels like returning to the relationship God has repeatedly convicted you about because being alone hurts.
It feels like hiding your faith because you desperately want the people around you to approve of you.
It feels like laughing at something that dishonors Christ because you do not want to become “that Christian.”
It feels like keeping the secret habit because, for a few minutes, it quiets something aching inside you.
It feels warm.
That is why you stay.
And somewhere nearby...
Jesus is being denied.
Peter stood with them.
Those words should bother us.
Not because Christians must never stand physically among unbelievers. Jesus Himself ate with sinners and intentionally went toward the lost.
The danger was not proximity.
The danger was what fear was doing inside Peter while he stood there.
He wanted to remain close enough to see what happened to Jesus...
but far enough away that nobody would identify him with Jesus.
Read that again.
Close enough to watch Jesus.
Far enough away to avoid the cost of belonging to Him.
There may be no more uncomfortable description of cultural Christianity.
We want Jesus close enough to save us.
Close enough to comfort us.
Close enough to bless our children.
Close enough to answer our prayers.
Close enough to give us heaven.
But sometimes...
not close enough to embarrass us.
Not close enough to interfere with the relationship.
Not close enough to confront the addiction.
Not close enough to determine how we spend our money.
Not close enough to govern what we watch.
Not close enough to change what we post.
Not close enough to make us different when everybody around us is warming themselves at the same fire.
Then somebody looked at Peter.
“You are not also one of this Man’s disciples, are you?”
There it was.
The moment.
Peter did not need a sermon.
He did not need another miracle.
He did not need more evidence.
He needed courage to say one sentence.
Yes.
I belong to Jesus.
Instead:
“I am not.”
Three words in many English translations.
A lifetime of confidence collapsing in seconds.
And Peter remained near the fire.
Then another accusation came.
Another denial.
Then another.
The Gospel accounts together show the pressure intensifying until Peter’s denial becomes emphatic.
And then...
a rooster crowed.
Luke gives us a detail that can break your heart if you allow yourself to see it.
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
Imagine that moment.
Peter hears the rooster.
Then he sees Jesus.
Not an abstract theological idea.
Not a stained-glass Christ.
Jesus.
Bruised.
Arrested.
Rejected.
Standing on the road toward suffering and crucifixion.
And Peter suddenly remembers.
Jesus had told him this would happen.
Before the rooster crowed, Peter would deny Him three times.
Peter had argued.
Peter had been certain of himself.
Peter thought his love was stronger than his weakness.
Then the courtyard exposed him.
Scripture says Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Those tears were not falling from the eyes of an unbeliever who had never cared about Jesus.
They came from a disciple who loved Jesus and had just discovered something terrifying about himself.
He was not as strong as he thought he was.
Maybe that is where this story has found you.
You love Jesus.
But you failed Him.
You knew better.
You promised yourself you would never return.
Then you returned.
You said it was the last time.
It was not.
You told God you were finished hiding.
Then you hid again.
You lifted your hands in worship while carrying something nobody in the room knew about.
You posted Scripture while privately struggling to obey it.
You encouraged everybody else while your own soul quietly unraveled.
And somewhere inside you is the same unbearable thought Peter may have carried:
After what I did...
how could Jesus still want me?
But Peter’s story does not end beside that fire.
And neither does the Gospel.
Jesus was crucified.
The Shepherd Peter denied did not deny Peter.
Christ went willingly to the cross, bearing sin and shame, and He rose from the grave.
And then John gives us another scene.
Another morning.
Another shoreline.
Another fire.
John 21:9 says that when the disciples came ashore, they saw ἀνθρακιὰν — anthrakian, a charcoal fire.
The same distinctive Greek noun used for the charcoal fire in John 18 appears again in John 21.
Do not rush past that.
The first charcoal fire was in the courtyard where Peter denied Jesus.
The second charcoal fire was on the shore where the risen Jesus met Peter.
John does not explicitly tell us, “Jesus made this charcoal fire to recreate Peter’s failure,” so we should not pretend Scripture says what it does not say.
But John unmistakably places the same rare image before us again.
A charcoal fire.
Peter had smelled that smoke before.
Imagine what that scent might have awakened.
A courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
“I am not.”
A rooster.
A look.
Tears.
Regret has smells.
Regret has sounds.
Regret remembers rooms.
Sometimes years can pass, and one song, one street, one photograph, one name, one smell can suddenly transport you back to the place where you became someone you wish you had never been.
And now Peter was standing near charcoal again.
Except this time...
Jesus was waiting for him there.
This is grace.
Jesus did not merely meet Peter somewhere completely disconnected from his failure.
John places restoration in the shadow of an image associated with Peter’s worst night.
But something had changed.
At the first fire, Peter was trying to warm himself while Jesus suffered.
At the second fire, Jesus had prepared breakfast.
At the first fire, Peter was questioned about his relationship with Jesus.
At the second fire, Jesus questioned Peter Himself.
At the first fire came denial.
At the second came restoration and commission.
“Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?”
Peter answers.
Jesus asks again.
Then again.
Three times.

We should be careful not to force every detail into an equation John never explicitly explains. Yet the narrative correspondence is impossible to ignore: Peter’s threefold denial is followed, after the resurrection, by a threefold questioning centered on his love for Christ and Jesus’ commission to care for His flock.
Jesus was not humiliating Peter for entertainment.
He was restoring a fallen disciple.
Grace does not always pretend the wound never happened.
Sometimes Jesus brings you back to the place you would rather forget...
not to destroy you there...
but to show you that your failure does not get the final word.
Peter had said three times, in effect:
I do not belong to Him.
Now the risen Christ gives him the opportunity to confess:
Lord, You know that I love You.
And Jesus keeps answering with purpose.
Feed My lambs.
Tend My sheep.
Feed My sheep.
In other words:
Peter...
you failed Me.
But I am not finished with you.
The scandal is real.
But grace is greater.
This is not cheap grace.
Jesus does not tell Peter that denying Him did not matter.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Obedience matters.
Following Jesus can cost us everything.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing to every repentant sinner who believes:
your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
Jesus does.
Peter would eventually stand publicly and proclaim the Christ he had once publicly denied.
The frightened man beside the courtyard fire would become a bold witness to the resurrection.
Not because Peter discovered hidden greatness inside himself.
Because Jesus restored him.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not the story of weak people discovering that they were secretly strong all along.
It is the story of sinners discovering that Christ is sufficient.
Peter's confidence in Peter had to die.
His confidence in Christ would become something altogether different.
Maybe yours must too.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove to God that you are worthy of another chance.
Stop.
You are not saved because you finally become impressive enough for Jesus.
You are saved by grace through faith because Jesus Christ is enough.
Repentance does not mean pretending the fire never happened.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
There is a fire somewhere in your life right now.
You know what it is.
The place you go when following Jesus feels cold.
The approval you cannot seem to surrender.
The person whose acceptance matters too much.
The private habit that promises comfort and leaves chains.
The screen.
The secret conversation.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The pride.
The resentment.
The applause.
The hidden compromise.
The carefully maintained Christian appearance covering a heart slowly wandering away.
You keep telling yourself:
I am only getting warm.
Peter probably was too.
But eventually somebody asks the question every life must answer:
Do you belong to Jesus?
Not:
Do you occasionally attend church?
Not:
Do you share Christian posts?
Not:
Were your parents Christians?
Not:
Do you believe God probably exists?
Do you belong to Jesus Christ?
Because there comes a moment when standing around the fire without answering becomes an answer of its own.
And perhaps this article found you while your hands were already stretched toward something you know cannot save you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not calling you away from the enemy’s fire because He wants you freezing in darkness.
He is calling you to Himself.
There is another fire.
There is another table.
There is bread.
There is mercy.
There is forgiveness.
There is restoration.
There is a risen Savior waiting for repentant sinners.
Peter discovered something beside those two fires that some of us spend decades trying to understand:
the world can warm your hands while your soul grows cold.
Jesus can confront your sin while restoring your soul.
That is the difference between condemnation and redemption.
The enemy says:
“Look what you did. Hide from God.”
The Gospel says:
“Look what Christ has done. Come home.”
The enemy says:
“You denied Him.”
Grace says:
“Repent, and look at the One who never denied His mission to rescue sinners.”
The enemy points toward your courtyard.
Jesus points toward His cross.
The enemy keeps replaying your failure.
Jesus shows you His scars.
And those scars declare that forgiveness was not purchased cheaply.
It was purchased with blood.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you know exactly what your fire is.
Do not anesthetize it.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes the first crack in a life of hiding is finally becoming honest.
Then pray.
Repent.
Talk to a mature believer.
Open Scripture.
Get accountable.
Do not turn a comment section into a substitute for discipleship.
Let honesty become the doorway into obedience.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
God is not indebted to anyone who supports a ministry.
But if this truth helped you, sharing it can place the Gospel in front of someone whose hands may be warming themselves beside the wrong fire tonight.
Someone may be ashamed.
Someone may be hiding.
Someone may think Jesus could never receive them again.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
Because one day the courtyard may become cold again, and you may need to remember where Peter's story actually ended.
Your support helps us keep producing resources intended to point people away from themselves and toward Jesus Christ.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Then invite your family.
Invite the friend who is drifting.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who has questions.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Even invite the unbelieving friend willing to hear what Christianity actually says about sin, grace, forgiveness and Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone is standing beside Peter.
The fire feels warm.
The crowd feels safer than confession.
And Jesus seems just far enough away that denial feels survivable.
But the rooster will eventually crow.
Every counterfeit fire eventually grows cold.
And when it does, remember this:
The Savior who knew Peter would deny Him was already preparing the grace that would restore him.
Your scandal does not have to become your ending.
Your failure does not have to become your name.
Your courtyard does not have to become your grave.
There is another fire waiting on the shore.
And the risen Jesus is still calling broken people back to Himself.
